claims.text: Service-regime thermal exposure triggers transformation of the metastable solid solution.
The transformation proceeds by diffusion-controlled, time-dependent nucleation and growth.
The transformation produces discrete ordered intermetallic precipitates involving Mg and a second major element.
Intermetallic precipitates nucleate both at grain boundaries and within grains.
Fine, uniformly dispersed intermetallic precipitates promote high-temperature oxidation resistance by stabilizing protective oxides.
Coarsened or interconnected intermetallic precipitates increase microgalvanic corrosion.
The initial alloy is a non-equilibrium metastable solid solution.
Thermally activated diffusion of Mg and associated elements promotes ordered-intermetallic nucleation and growth.
Fine and coherent precipitates assist formation of a stable protective oxide scale.
Coarsened or interconnected precipitates create microgalvanic couples that locally break down passivation.
Thermal aging will produce detectable new Mg-rich intermetallic phases relative to the initial state.
If the new intermetallic particles remain fine and well distributed, the aged alloy will form a more protective oxide scale than the initial alloy.
Intermetallic coarsening will coincide with increased localized corrosion.
On balance, aging is predicted to improve high-temperature oxidation resistance while potentially compromising corrosion resistance.
The precise transformation kinetics and critical precipitate size or distribution thresholds are unknown.
TEM/EDS, oxidation testing, and electrochemical testing can compare intermetallic formation, scale integrity, and corrosion behavior between aged and unaged specimens.
